https://www.thetimes.com/uk/get-britain-.text: Accessibility Links THE FUNDAY TIMES Travel the world from just £7.99 with these brilliant books Whether you’re reading by a pool on holiday or in the local park, there’s no limit to how many miles your mind can travel Julie Broadbent and Verity Robinson Saturday July 18 2026, 3.00pm BST , The Sunday Times Listen 0:00 / • 14:53 min Share Share this article Email Twitter Facebook Link Save S ummer is here, and for many that means jetting off to foreign shores and new horizons. But really the only things you need to travel the world are your mind and a good book. This brilliant selection, chosen by Julie Broadbent, the School Library Association’s secondary school librarian of the year 2025, and Verity Robinson, primary school librarian of the year 2025, takes readers from Scotland to Papua New Guinea and Poland to the Amazon rainforest, via a high-octane train journey across the US and an unlikely friendship in Cambodia. Most commented 1 Prince and Princess of Wales release video for George’s 13th birthday Royal family 443 comments 2 Bloomsbury gets payout in .5bn Anthropic copyright case Companies & Markets 54 comments 3 Wetherspoons issues fourth profit warning, citing costs and sales Companies & Markets 47 comments 4 Pep Guardiola: Italy prepared to break the bank to lure new coach Football 55 comments 5 ‘Attack dog’ drones unveiled to fly alongside RAF jets Defence 67 comments So sit back, strap in and get ready to discover new countries, cultures and incredible stories. Papua New Guinea The Shark Caller by Zillah Bethell Blue Wing is desperate to become a “shark caller”, but when a visiting family arrives, she is told she must befriend their daughter, Maple. At first the girls don’t get on, but with time — and the lure of ancient treasure — they become firm friends. Immersed in the sights, sounds and ancient traditions of Papua New Guinea, readers will be enthralled by this adventure. £7.99 Usborne 9+ Ethiopia The Fastest Boy in the World by Elizabeth Laird Eleven-year-old Solomon loves to run and dreams of winning an Olympic gold medal. But when his grandfather takes him to Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, Solomon finds himself running the most important race of his life. A moving story about resilience, strength and family that brilliantly captures the people and culture of Ethiopia. £7.99 Macmillan Children’s Books 7-10 Advertisement Costa Rica Turtle Moon by Hannah Gold Silver and her family move to a turtle rescue centre in Costa Rica. When poachers steal the eggs of a rare leatherback turtle, Silver and her friend Rafi go on a dangerous mission to catch the thieves. This thought-provoking eco-adventure will take the reader on an unforgettable journey through the country’s vibrant, perilous jungles. £7.99 HarperCollins 8+ Japan Tsunami Girl by Julian Sedgwick, illustrated by Chie Kutsuwada After being caught in the devastating 2011 tsunami, Yuki must come to terms with the trauma of what has happened to her. To find solace she returns to the devastation of her grandfather’s house to lay the ghosts of the past to rest. A coming-of-age story combining prose and manga. £10.99 Guppy Books 12+ India Tamarind and the Star of Ishta by Jasbinder Bilan Tamarind’s mum died soon after she was born, but when her father remarries, she is sent to her mum’s ancestral home to reconnect with her extended family. Set in the foothills of the Indian Himalayas, it couldn’t be more different from her home in England. A remarkable story filled with mystery, intrigue and family myth. £7.99 Chicken House 9-14 Read more from The Funday Times Read an exclusive extract from the new Impossible Creatures book Get colouring to win a brilliant Gruffalo book bundle! Are you clever enough to be a spy? Try these puzzles from GCHQ The United States Kidnap on the California Comet by MG Leonard and Sam Sedgman, illustrated by Elisa Paganelli Join Harrison “Hal” Beck and his Uncle Nat as they travel across the US from Chicago to San Francisco by train to interview a billionaire. But when the billionaire’s daughter, Marianne, is kidnapped, Hal must try to rescue her. £7.99 Macmillan Children’s Books 9-11 South Africa The White Giraffe by Lauren St John After a family tragedy, 11-year-old Martine is sent to live with a grandmother she has never met on a wildlife reserve near Cape Town, South Africa. Leaving everything familiar behind, she discovers a world of breathtaking landscapes, remarkable animals and ancient mysteries. A fast-paced and captivating read, perfect for animal lovers. £8.99 Orion 9+ Advertisement The Amazon The Explorer by Katherine Rundell An aircraft crashes deep in the Amazon rainforest. Four children survive. With no equipment, no food and no way of knowing how to get back to civilisation, they must adapt to their dangerous surroundings and rely on each other to survive. Filled with detailed descriptions of the Amazon featuring piranhas, snakes, wildfires and caimans. £8.99 Bloomsbury 8-11 Jamaica When Life Gives You Mangos by Kereen Getten Clara is struggling with amnesia after a mysterious event from the previous summer, but when Rudy arrives from England things begin to change. As the pair explore the island together, they uncover long-buried secrets that may hold the key to Clara’s past. Rich in the beauty of Jamaica’s landscapes, oceans and communities, this captivating adventure celebrates friendship, kindness and belonging. £7.99 Pushkin Press 8-12 Nigeria One Chance Dance by Efua Traoré Jomi hasn’t heard from his mum since she left their rural village in Nigeria for Lagos — the only clue he has is that she loved a TV dance competition based in the city. With great courage he embarks on an epic adventure to reunite with his mum. This heartwarming story brings the vibrancy of the city and its culture to life. £7.99 Chicken House 9+ Kurdistan to the Netherlands The Bicycle by Patricia McCormick and Mevan Babakar, illustrated by Yas Imamura Mevan and her parents are refugees. Wherever they travel — Turkey, Azerbaijan, Russia — they feel small and unwelcome. But when they reach the Netherlands, a stranger gifts Mevan a bicycle that makes her feel “a hundred feet tall”. A real celebration of the importance of empathy wherever you find yourselves. £7.99 HarperCollins 3-7 Cambodia Lost on Gibbon Island by Jess Butterworth, illustrated by Rob Biddulph Lark and her family are on a research trip when she finds herself shipwrecked on an island with only a baby gibbon for company. Facing heat, hunger and a lack of fresh water, Lark must rely on her courage and resourcefulness to survive and get back to her family. Told through diary entries, the story is an extraordinary tale of survival and explores themes including environmental conservation and the illegal animal smuggling trade. £7.99 Orion 9+ Advertisement Caribbean Clean Up! by Nathan Bryon and Dapo Adeola Rocket is visiting her grandparents in the Caribbean when a baby turtle washes up on the beach, tangled in plastic. She decides she must do something and enlists the help of everyone on the beach to join the clean-up crew — and learns that she can make a huge difference. £7.99 Puffin 3-6 Ireland The Tree That Sang to Me by Serena Molloy In Ireland, Kai finds comfort from his troubling family life in the branches of a sycamore tree. When a girl called Sky starts climbing Kai’s tree, he learns how powerful having a friend to talk to can be. An emotive story written in verse, this book covers themes of mental health and a family separated through the criminal justice system, with a dyslexia-friendly typeface. £7.99 Hodder 9+ Pakistan The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain When Zubair, the youngest of seven brothers, discovers he has the ability to time travel, he uses his power to try to save his parents’ marriage. The story blends laugh-out-loud episodes with exciting plot twists. Themes of partition, arranged marriage, divorce and family struggles are also tackled perfectly for young readers. £8.99 Puffin 8-12 France Safiyyah’s War by Hiba Noor Khan In Nazi-occupied Paris, Safiyyah unravels the mysteries behind her father’s resistance work and joins her community’s efforts in helping others in their time of need. Inspired by the true story of hundreds of Jews being helped to safety in the Grand Mosque during the Second World War, this story shines a light on the power of compassion. £7.99 Andersen Press 9+ Egypt Secrets of a Sun King by Emma Carroll After Lil finds a mysterious package on her grandad’s doorstep just as he’s struck down by illness, she decides she must return it to where it came from: Egypt. A thrilling adventure interwoven with a subplot from ancient Egyptian times, this tale will have its readers reaching for the history books. £7.99 Faber 9-12 Advertisement The Arctic The Last Bear by Hannah Gold, illustrated by Levi Pinfold The first of Gold’s novels with strong environmental messages, The Last Bear is a book that children and adults will struggle to put down. April and her dad have the unique opportunity to spend six months in the Arctic. When April meets the last polar bear on the island, she does everything she can to ensure it is protected. Beautifully illustrated by Levi Pinfold. £12.99 HarperCollins 9-12 Poland The Dragon in the Bookshop by Ewa Jozefkowicz Konrad and Maya find themselves whisked back in time in this beautifully told adventure that mixes contemporary life with ancient Polish folk tales. There is plenty to love about this story, which teaches us how bravery can sometimes mean asking for help. And there’s a dragon. Just magical. £7.99 Zephyr 9-12 Scotland A Kind of Spark by Elle McNicoll When 11-year-old Addie learns about the witch trials in her Scottish home town centuries ago, she begins campaigning for a memorial in their honour. Addie is autistic and often sees the world differently to others — she knows there is more to the stories of the “witches” than people realise, just like her own. A book everyone should read. £7.99 Macmillan Children’s Books 9-11 Kenya When Stars Are Scattered by Victoria Jamieson and Omar Mohamed The true story of Omar and his brother, Hassan, growing up in a Kenyan refugee camp, this graphic novel puts into perspective how grateful we should all be for the small things we take for granted. A useful read for developing empathy and understanding the refugee crises happening in the world. £10.99 Faber 9-12 Syria Nour’s Secret Library by Wafa’ Tarnowska, illustrated by Vali Mintzi Based on true events during the Syrian civil war, this book follows two young children as they create a community library that becomes a beacon of hope for its readers, who find distraction, comfort and safety between the pages of the books. £7.99 Barefoot Books 6-10 Advertisement Worldwide What a Wonderful Word by Nicola Edwards and Luisa Uribe A collection of “untranslatable” words from around the world that will give readers a glimpse into the lives of those who use them. In Italy abbiocco is the “drowsiness from eating a big meal”, while pochemuchka is Russian for “a child who asked ‘why?’” all the time. Filled with endearing illustrations from Luisa Uribe. £9.99 Little Tiger 7+ Worldwide Hike It by Iron Tazz If you enjoy nature and want to learn skills for the outdoors, this book by Iron Tazz, an American hiker, is packed with tips, from tackling 30 different terrains to being mindful in nature and packing lightweight luggage. £20 Magic Cat 7+ Worldwide Journeys: Tales of Travel and Trailblazers by Jonathan Litton, illustrated by Chris Chalik, Dave Shephard, Jon Davis and Leo Hartas This wonderfully illustrated book looks at how humans have historically travelled on water, land, ice, snow and by man-made machinery. From ancient travellers in China to fearless flyers like Amelia Earhart, each story is unique and inspiring. £17.99 360 Degrees 7-12 Worldwide The Lost Book of Adventure: from the notebooks of the Unknown Adventurer by Teddy Keen A metal container is found in a remote part of the Amazon. In it we discover a collection of notebooks, journals and sketchbooks jam-packed with adventures and advice from the Unknown Adventurer. From surviving a Saharan dust storm to meeting an emperor penguin in Antarctica, readers will go on an unforgettable exploration of the natural world. £12.99 Quarto 7+ Top stories 1 Trump media company to charge 0,000 a month for fast access to posts US business 2 Queen Camilla marks birthday with gift of book for every Year 6 child Royal family Top stories 1 Trump agrees landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia US news 2 Tesla misses profit target and reports first cash burn in two years Companies & Markets 3 Jailed Hong Kong democracy leader told he is to be deported from UK Asia 4 Alphabet earnings boosted by Google Cloud’s strong growth Companies & Markets 5 Joanna Pettet obituary: actress who escaped early death Obituaries sla.org.uk Best books Share Share this article Email Twitter Facebook Link Save Promoted Content Previous Article Next Article The Flash Sale £1 for 3 months Enjoy unlimited access to all articles. https://www.politico.eu/article/latvia-p.text: RIGA — Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs wants Brussels to hand over €7 billion to help cover the military and economic costs of confronting Russia, as pressure grows over the price of the country’s hard line on Moscow. The money should come from the EU’s next seven-year budget , under a new Competitiveness Fund , to offset higher defense spending and the collapse in trade with Russia since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kulbergs told POLITICO's Brussels Playbook in an interview. The cash, which Riga wants to come on top of other funds earmarked for the country, would amount to almost half of Latvia’s projected €15.1 billion defense bill over the seven-year budget period. Advertisement Advertisement The demand comes at a sensitive moment. Latvia has been one of Europe’s staunchest supporters of Ukraine, sharply increasing defense spending since Moscow's full-scale invasion, even as sanctions and the collapse of bilateral trade have cut deeply into economic links that once ran eastward. But ahead of an Oct. 3 national election , parties arguing that Riga should demand more in return for sanctions and military support are gaining ground. The European Commission has proposed substantially increasing EU-level defense funding in the 2028-2034 budget, including a €125.2 billion security, defense industry and space pot in the European Competitiveness Fund. That money is designed to finance projects across the bloc rather than provide Latvia with a pre-agreed €7 billion allocation, and the entire budget remains subject to negotiations between EU governments and the European Parliament. Kulbergs argues that Latvia deserves special consideration because it is borrowing to provide security for countries much farther from the front line. “We are getting our budget deficit to the maximum […] and from that debt we're paying […] the defense of the whole [of] Europe,” the prime minister said at the government chancellery. Much of Latvia’s military spending ultimately flows back to richer Western European economies, Kulbergs added, pointing to arms purchases from Germany, France, Spain, Sweden and the Netherlands. “We fuel their economies,” he added. Election pressure A sharper version of the same argument is emerging on the campaign trail. Ainārs Šlesers, a veteran populist businessman whose party sits with the far-right Patriots for Europe group in Brussels, says Latvia should demand compensation when it backs EU sanctions on Russia. Šlesers condemns Moscow’s invasion and says support for Ukraine should continue, but argues that Latvia cannot absorb the costs indefinitely. Advertisement Advertisement “We are losing money … we are talking about how to support Ukraine, but we are a victim,” he told POLITICO at his Riga campaign headquarters. When EU sanctions come up for renewal, Šlesers said Latvia should “get in return support.” Asked whether that could mean withholding Riga’s backing for sanctions, he stopped short of threatening a veto but did not rule it out. “I don't want to talk about [a] veto [now],” he said. “I guess that we [...] will find a peaceful solution.” Šlesers, who has business ties with Russian oligarchs , said the country needs to eventually restore economic ties with Moscow, and advocated for a quick end to the war. “There are things which we cannot replace because if it's your neighboring country and you're connected historically […] we need to find the right model.” He argued that whether to hand over territory to Russia should be "a decision by Ukraine" but argued that other countries have lost territory to Russia after conflicts, including Latvia, "to reach [a] peace agreement." Kulbergs’ center-right party currently leads the polls, but coalition arithmetic could determine how far Latvia’s Russia policy shifts after October. The far-right, pro-Russia Sovereign Power party, polling second, wants to restore ties with Moscow but is considered off-limits by mainstream parties. Šlesers, polling third, is a more plausible coalition partner — and Kulbergs has left the door open to governing with him. Advertisement Advertisement The center-left Progressives, polling fourth and also hoping to enter government with Kulbergs, warn that bringing Šlesers into the coalition would gradually soften Riga’s line on Russia. “I’m 100 percent sure Latvia’s foreign policy towards Russia is going to soften over time,” the party’s prime ministerial candidate Andris Šuvajevs told POLITICO outside parliament. He pointed to possible sanctions exemptions for Russian business interests and ministers “speaking in a more friendly tone towards Russia.” Tough on Russia Ahead of a new sanctions package due in the fall, Kulbergs called for a total EU visa ban on Russians. EU countries granted more than 630,000 visas to Russian citizens in 2025. In the last sanctions package, France and Italy resisted a blanket ban on Russian combatants, arguing this issue should be covered by EU visa rules rather than as part of sanctions, while northern and eastern countries pushed for tougher restrictions. The eventual deal created the legal and political basis for barring Russian combatants and ex-combatants who took part in the war — leaving it up to EU countries to decide when the ban would take effect. “Are we nuts?” said Kulbergs on the delay. “We allow Russian military soldiers to be given visas, the ones killing [Ukrainians] on the field.” He also urged EU countries to revisit sending Russia’s €210 billion in sovereign assets frozen in Europe to Ukraine, dismissing concerns Moscow could challenge the move after the war. Advertisement Advertisement Kulbergs also rebuked European Council President António Costa’s decision to open a communications channel with the Kremlin , saying doing so should be “a decision of all the countries together.” He called any Kremlin outreach “a useless exercise,” arguing there’s no sign President Vladimir Putin is ready to negotiate and that talks would merely give Russia "breathing time" to make its "next move." Despite Latvia severing ties with its eastern neighbor, and Kulbergs' hawkish position on relations with Moscow, he said “we have to be open” to reestablishing ties once Russia pays reparations to Ukraine and those responsible for war crimes face justice, pointing to postwar Germany as the example to follow. “Do we isolate Germany because of that? No, it's acceptance of guilt, acceptance of wrongdoing, punishment, and retribution," he said. After a ceasefire, Kulbergs concluded, "the insecurity of the border will only rise" as the real threat will be a wave of migration as hundreds of thousands of “screwed up” soldiers return from the battlefield seeking a better life and other citizens flee as Moscow's war economy crumbles.

https://www.dw.com/en/smuggling-suspecte.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mlz6 Orangutans in the wild are native only to Indonesia's Sumatra island and Borneo. These young ones were found in a forest in India Image: Odisha Forest Department/AFP Advertisement Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week. Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad. The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade. How did five baby orangutans end up in India? "The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC, told DW. "What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she asked. The youngsters appeared to be healthy and were being cared for at a zoo after their rescue Image: ANI/IMAGO The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state. "These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia. "We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest… by an international wildlife smuggling racket." Indian officials seize pythons, parrots, giant tortoises The orangutans are the latest in a series of exotic wildlife being seized in India. In November 2024, authorities in the Indian city of Bengaluru seized 40 rare animals arriving from the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, including Aldabra giant tortoises, gibbons, American alligators and iguanas. In June 2025, Mumbai Customs seized 284 exotic animals arriving in four consignments from the Thai capital, Bangkok, including snakes and tortoises. In July 2025, customs officials in the Indian city of Pune intercepted 20 exotic animals from passengers arriving from Bangkok. They included 14 green tree pythons, four double-eyed fig parrots and two Sumatran striped rabbits. 'Shocking' volume of trafficked wildlife found in India According to figures from TRAFFIC, 7,272 individual animals, alive and dead, were seized from passenger baggage in smuggling attempts between Thailand and India between January 2022 and May 2025, with more than 80% of interceptions taking place in India. The animals included reptiles, birds and mammals — many apparently destined for the exotic pet trade. "We have found hundreds of species and thousands of individuals being trafficked into India through air and land routes. This changed drastically from around 2020," conservation researcher and practitioner Uttara Mendiratta told DW. "Both the volume of this trafficking , and the number of species involved, many of which are endangered, have been shocking." Law enforcement lagging behind smugglers TRAFFIC says India and Malaysia were the countries most implicated in an illegal gibbon trade chain identified in 2025, with gibbons being moved from Malaysia to India. Trishala Ashok, a conservation filmmaker and science communicator, says the scale of the trade remains difficult to establish. "Our enforcement systems haven't evolved at the same speed as the trade," Ashok told DW. "We are still reacting to individual seizures rather than mapping the networks, financiers, suppliers and buyers behind them." Tito Joseph of the Wildlife Protection Society of India says the situation is escalating. "Smuggling of exotic species was always there in India," Joseph told DW. At the same time, he noted that it has increased significantly since 2018. He identifies routes running from Myanmar through northeast India into other parts of the country, as well as movement from Bangladesh into India. By air, Thailand and Malaysia are important sources of trafficked wildlife. The routes into India also extend beyond airports. Exotic animals are also reaching India through its northeastern land borders. "What is new is the large volume of incoming live wildlife. There are indications that some of the traders who were involved in smuggling live animals like star tortoises out are now also involved in sourcing [other] exotic wildlife," said Mendiratta, the conservation researcher. Social media fans illegal animal trade Demand is being fueled by growing ownership of exotic pets and unregulated digital marketplaces, according to a June 2026 analysis of India's exotic pet trade by Humane World for Animals India, an NGO that works to tackle the root causes of animal cruelty. "Internationally, social media platforms have aided and abetted the growth of illegal trade in wild animals by providing a platform for people to display and boast about the animals they collect," wildlife biologist and conservation scientist Ravi Chellam told DW. "These platforms are also serving as an online marketplace for the illegal trade to flourish." "The problem is exacerbated by the senseless and obscenely huge personal collections of animals from around the world by the rich and the famous," Chellam noted. Establishing where an animal came from can become particularly difficult once it has crossed several borders. "A seizure cannot be the end of the investigation. It should be the beginning," said Ashok, the conservation filmmaker. "Who supplied the animals? Who arranged the movement? Who paid? Who was waiting for them?" she asks. "Until we start following those links, we will keep catching consignments without dismantling the networks behind them." https://nltimes.nl/2026/09/14/fugitive-w.text: Image The police's FASTNL team arrested a 31-year-old man from Poland in Dinteloord, wanted for murdering his father in Poland. 9 September 2026 - Credit: Politie / Politie - License: All Rights Reserved Crime FASTNL Poland fugitive murder aggravated assault police arrest Dinteloord extradition » More tags « Less tags Monday, 14 September 2026 - 11:10 Share this article: Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Fugitive wanted for killing his father in Poland arrested in Dinteloord The police’s Fugitive Active Search Team (FASTNL) arrested a 31-year-old Polish man in Dinteloord last week. He is wanted in Poland for murdering his father and could face life in prison, the police reported on Monday. FASTNL arrested the man at his place of employment on Wednesday based on new information, the police said, without providing further details. According to the police, he was on the run for some time. The man is wanted in Poland for aggravated assault and murder. The victim was the suspect’s father. If convicted, he could face life in prison. Poland has requested the man’s extradition. He is in custody while that process is underway. FASTNL is affiliated with ENFAST, a partnership of fugitive-hunting teams from police forces across the European Union. In this partnership, the various police forces are able to share information about fugitives more quickly. “International cooperation is crucial, as an estimated majority of fugitives choose to hide outside their own national borders. This collaboration enables fugitives to be tracked down more quickly,” the police said.
